newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND'S KOLODKO OFFERS PLAN FOR ZLOTY EMS ACCESS.
newsitem.headline: POLAND'S KOLODKO OFFERS PLAN FOR ZLOTY EMS ACCESS.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko wants to peg the zloty to the ecu and limit its trading band on the domestic forex market to lead the Polish unit into the European Monetary System (EMS) over the next 10 years.

Kolodko on Tuesday presented to reporters the plan of stabilising the zloty as part of his new Euro 2006 scheme aimed at bringing Poland, aspiring for European Union membership, to join the European Monetary Union.
In its initial phase the plan assumes that the peg for the zloty exchange rate would gradually move from the basket of five western currencies to the ecu and later to the Euro.

The zloty is now devalued at a monthly rate of one percent against a basket of currencies made up in 45 percent of the U.S. dollar, in 35 percent of the German mark, and in 10 percent of the pound sterling.
Swiss and French francs have a five percent share each.
The first step of the plan, which Kolodko said would likely be implemented over 1998-2004, would be to replace the four European currencies in the basket with the euro.
The second phase would be to phase out the monthly devaluation of the zloty's central parity rate but keep it floating within the current 14-percent band on the domestic foreign exchange market.
The plan envisages a possibility of a one-off devaluation of the parity rate to maintain, if need be, the competitiveness of Polish exports.
The final step would be to limit the zloty's trading space to 2.25 percent on both sides of the parity rate against the current seven percent, as in the EMS.
"Such a shaping of an NBP (the central bank) policy would enhance the credibility and strength of the Polish currency as well as permit, in time, the zloty to join the EMS," Kolodko said.
Asked for a timetable for the plan's implementation Kolodko said:
"Time is not ripe yet to discuss specific schedules but one could expect it(the process)...to span over 1998-2004 and the key efforts to centre during the 1998-2000 period."

The Euro 2006 plan assumes that by 2005 Poland will be able to meet all EMU membership criteria concerning the level of budget deficits and public debt, inflation, interest rates levels and exchange rate stability.
